summary.text: Letting \(w=e^{2\pi i/13}\), Euler’s formula gives \(4\cos^2(\pi k/13)=2+w^k+w^{-k}=2+w^k+w^{13-k}\). Expanding the six factors and reducing the elementary symmetric sums using \(w^{13}=1\) and \(1+w+\cdots+w^{12}=0\) yields respectively \(11,45,84,70,21,1\), with the alternating signs supplied by the product expansion.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
P(x)=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6.
\]
We prove that
\[
P(x)=\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\!\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right).
\]

Introduce the primitive thirteenth root of unity
\[
\zeta=e^{2\pi i/13}.
\]
Then \(\zeta^{13}=1\), and \(\zeta\ne1\). Indeed, \(e^{2\pi i/13}=1\) would require \(2\pi/13\) to be an integral multiple of \(2\pi\), which is impossible. Consequently the geometric-series identity gives
\[
1+\zeta+\zeta^2+\cdots+\zeta^{12}
=\frac{\zeta^{13}-1}{\zeta-1}=0.
\tag{1}
\]
More generally, for each \(k=1,\dots,6\), put \(\eta=\zeta^k\). Since \(1\le k<13\), \(\eta\ne1\), while \(\eta^{13}=1\). Therefore
\[
1+\eta+\eta^2+\cdots+\eta^{12}=0.
\tag{2}
\]

We next derive the polynomial satisfied by \(u=\eta+\eta^{-1}\). For \(n\ge0\), set
\[
S_n=\eta^n+\eta^{-n}.
\]
Thus \(S_0=2\), \(S_1=u\), and multiplication by \(u=\eta+\eta^{-1}\) gives
\[
uS_n=(\eta+\eta^{-1})(\eta^n+\eta^{-n})
=S_{n+1}+S_{n-1}.
\]
Hence
\[
S_{n+1}=uS_n-S_{n-1}.
\tag{3}
\]
Successive use of this recurrence yields
\[
\begin{aligned}
S_1&=u,\\
S_2&=u^2-2,\\
S_3&=u^3-3u,\\
S_4&=u^4-4u^2+2,\\
S_5&=u^5-5u^3+5u,\\
S_6&=u^6-6u^4+9u^2-2.
\end{aligned}
\tag{4}
\]

Multiply (2) by \(\eta^{-6}\). Since the exponents then range from \(-6\) to \(6\), and inverse powers can be paired, we obtain
\[
0=\sum_{j=-6}^{6}\eta^j
=1+\sum_{n=1}^{6}(\eta^n+\eta^{-n})
=1+S_1+S_2+S_3+S_4+S_5+S_6.
\tag{5}
\]
Substituting the expressions in (4) into (5) and collecting like powers of \(u\) gives
\[
u^6+u^5-5u^4-4u^3+6u^2+3u-1=0.
\tag{6}
\]
Thus, for every \(k=1,\dots,6\), the number
\[
u_k=\zeta^k+\zeta^{-k}
\]
is a root of
\[
q(U)=U^6+U^5-5U^4-4U^3+6U^2+3U-1.
\tag{7}
\]

Now define
\[
y_k=u_k+2=\zeta^k+\zeta^{-k}+2.
\]
Replacing \(U\) by \(T-2\) in (7), a binomial expansion gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
q(T-2)
&=(T-2)^6+(T-2)^5-5(T-2)^4-4(T-2)^3\\
&\qquad+6(T-2)^2+3(T-2)-1\\
&=T^6-11T^5+45T^4-84T^3+70T^2-21T+1.
\end{aligned}
\tag{8}
\]
Therefore each \(y_k\), for \(1\le k\le6\), is a root of the monic polynomial
\[
p(T)=T^6-11T^5+45T^4-84T^3+70T^2-21T+1.
\tag{9}
\]

These six roots are distinct. To see this in real terms, Euler's formula gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
y_k
&=e^{2\pi i k/13}+e^{-2\pi i k/13}+2\\
&=2\cos\left(\frac{2\pi k}{13}\right)+2\\
&=4\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right),
\end{aligned}
\tag{10}
\]
where the last equality is \(2+2\cos(2\theta)=4\cos^2\theta\). For \(1\le k\le6\), the angles \(\pi k/13\) all lie strictly between \(0\) and \(\pi/2\). On this interval cosine is positive and strictly decreasing, so its square is also strictly decreasing. Hence the six values \(y_1,\dots,y_6\) are pairwise distinct.

The monic degree-six polynomial \(p(T)\) has the six distinct roots \(y_1,\dots,y_6\). By the factor theorem, each \(T-y_k\) divides \(p(T)\); because the roots are distinct, their product divides \(p(T)\). Both the product and \(p\) are monic of degree six, so they are equal:
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{6}(T-y_k)
=T^6-11T^5+45T^4-84T^3+70T^2-21T+1.
\tag{11}
\]
Equivalently, the elementary symmetric functions of the six numbers \(y_k\) are
\[
e_0=1,\qquad e_1=11,\qquad e_2=45,\qquad e_3=84,
\qquad e_4=70,\qquad e_5=21,\qquad e_6=1.
\tag{12}
\]
This is precisely the coefficient computation obtained by reducing powers of \(\zeta\) using \(\zeta^{13}=1\) and \(1+\zeta+\cdots+\zeta^{12}=0\): the recurrence (3) and the expansion (8) provide an explicit compact derivation of all seven reductions.

Finally, homogenize (11). Namely, replace \(T\) by \(S/X\) and multiply by \(X^6\), or simply compare the elementary-symmetric expansion. This gives the polynomial identity in two variables
\[
\prod_{k=1}^{6}(S-y_kX)
=S^6-11S^5X+45S^4X^2-84S^3X^3+70S^2X^4-21SX^5+X^6.
\tag{13}
\]
Setting \(S=1\) and using (10), we conclude
\[
\begin{aligned}
\prod_{k=1}^{6}\left(1-4\cos^2\left(\frac{\pi k}{13}\right)x\right)
&=\prod_{k=1}^{6}(1-y_kx)\\
&=1-11x+45x^2-84x^3+70x^4-21x^5+x^6.
\end{aligned}
\]
This is the required factorization of the denominator.
